verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, on Shoshannim, of the sons of Korah, a Maskil, a song of loves.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung to the tune called Lilies: a psalm of the sons of Korah, a teaching-song, a song of love.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the title, numbered as verse 0 in the KJV. It is performance instructions, like a program note. The choirmaster is the Temple music leader, the Korahites are a family of Levite singers, and 'Shoshannim' (lilies) probably names a tune or an instrument, since Radak and Metzudat Zion call it a musical instrument shaped like a lily. Rashi instead hears a metaphor for gentle, fragrant scholars. Maskil is another musical or literary label of uncertain sense, taken by Meiri as 'something that wakes the heart to attention'. The KJV leaves 'Maschil' untranslated and renders yedidot as 'loves', which is closer to the plural 'beloved ones' or 'love songs' than to a single romance. Rashi and the Targum read the plural as applying to the scholars or the sanhedrin. The Hebrew does not say who wrote the lyric, but it does say the words are for a wedding-style song.

philological_notes.note: 'On lilies': probably a tune name or instrument, as in the heading of Psalms 69 and 80. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as an instrument; Rashi as a figure for scholars.
A plural of 'beloved' or 'love'; Ibn Ezra glosses it 'like ahavot', loves.

verses.translation_literal: My heart is astir with a good word; I am saying: my works are for a king; my tongue is the stylus of a swift scribe.
verses.translation_dramatic: Something stirs in my heart, a good word, rising like water in a spring. I speak now, and what I have made I make for a king. My tongue is a scribe's reed pen, and it will not stumble.
verses.directors_commentary: The poet speaks first, in his own voice, and sets the frame: this is a court song, and he is its craftsman. The verb rachash occurs only here; it means a gentle, bubbling motion (Rashi and Meiri tie it to the rustling of moving things, and Metzudat Zion to the 'pan' offering that sizzles in Leviticus 2:7). The KJV's 'inditing' is a dead archaism for 'dictating', and it hides the physical image of something simmering. 'Good word' means more than 'a good matter': davar is both word and thing, and the pun is the point of the poet's boast. The 'stylus' (et) is a scribe's reed pen; Egyptian and Canaanite scribes were professionals who wrote fast on papyrus or sherds, so 'swift scribe' is a claim of trained skill, not of haste. Note that the poet says 'my works', plural, though the KJV gives the awkward 'things which I have made touching the king'; the preposition is simply 'for the king'.

philological_notes.note: A hapax: to stir, bubble, seethe. Rashi says it means movement or swarming; Metzudat Zion links it to the sizzling pan-offering.
A scribe's stylus. Metzudat Zion compares 'iron stylus' in Job 19:24.

verses.translation_literal: You are beautiful, more than the sons of man; grace is poured on your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are fairer than any son of Adam. Grace has been poured out upon your lips like oil from a jar, and so God has blessed you, and the blessing does not end.
verses.directors_commentary: The poet now turns to the king and speaks 'you' to him. Two compliments are paired: his looks and his speech. The verb yafeyafita is a doubled form, an intensive of 'beautiful' (Ibn Ezra and Meiri debate this; most read it as emphatic), so the KJV's flat 'fairer' lightly understates it. 'Poured' (hutzak) is the verb for pouring molten metal or anointing oil, and Ibn Ezra notes the link to 'they poured upon the offering', so the king's speech is imagined as liquid, valuable and shaped. The 'sons of man' (benei adam) is simply 'humankind'. A king's persuasive speech was part of his job in a court where he judged cases in person. 'Therefore' (al-ken) is the logical pivot that runs through the next verses: the blessing is the result, not the cause. The KJV 'thou art fairer' is archaic but accurate; the Targum, as given in the packet, makes the king the Messiah and the lips prophetic, which is its reading, not the Hebrew's.

philological_notes.note: A reduplicated verb, probably intensive: 'you are exceedingly beautiful'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri discuss whether doubling shows excess or weakness (as in 'reddish') and conclude here it strengthens.
Hophal of yatzaq, 'to pour (oil, metal)'; the passive suggests grace was given, not earned.

verses.translation_literal: Gird your sword on [your] thigh, O mighty one, your splendor and your majesty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bind on your sword, warrior, let it hang at your thigh, for it is your splendor, and your majesty.
verses.directors_commentary: A king in the ancient Near East was first a war leader, and the sword at the thigh was the badge of the role; right-handed men wore it on the left hip so the right hand could draw across the body (Ehud wore his on the right thigh because he was left-handed, Judges 3:16). The line is a command, almost a ceremony: the king is being dressed. 'Splendor and majesty' (hod and hadar) are the two royal words, used in the Psalms for God as well (Psalm 96:6). The KJV's 'most mighty, with thy glory' turns a bare apposition into a clause; the Hebrew simply sets 'your splendor and your majesty' after the sword, as if naming it. Ibn Ezra treats 'gibbor' as 'you are the mighty one'. Meiri says the sword at the thigh is a conquering king's emblem. The Targum puts killing into it, which the Hebrew does not.

philological_notes.note: Imperative: to gird or belt on. Radak says swords are worn at the loins or on the thigh.
Paired royal attributes, 'splendor and majesty'; Rashi says the sword is the splendor, i.e. the scholar's war of Torah.

verses.translation_literal: And your majesty: prosper, ride, on a word of truth and humility-righteousness; and your right hand will teach you awesome [deeds].
verses.translation_dramatic: And your majesty, let it go on and prosper. Ride out for the sake of truth, and of humble righteousness. Let your right hand teach you deeds that make the watchers tremble.
verses.directors_commentary: The Hebrew repeats 'and your majesty': the phrase closes verse 4 in pause (hodkha vahadarekha) and opens verse 5 again (vahadarekha), a repetition at the seam that ties the two verses together, so play the second as an echo of the first. The KJV's 'in thy majesty ride prosperously' gets there by treating the word as 'in thy majesty'; Ibn Ezra explains such a reading as a missing bet (u-vehadarkha), but the Hebrew has no preposition. It also folds two commands, 'prosper, ride' (tzelach, rekhav), into one adverb. A king rode to war on a chariot or horse, yet the cause named here is not conquest but 'a word of truth and humility-righteousness' (davar emet ve'anvah-tzedek). 'Anvah' (humility) is an odd word beside a king; the KJV's 'meekness' is accurate. Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss whether it is 'humility of righteousness' or two separate virtues, and Radak notes the irregular spelling with a final he. Radak adds that the king's chariot is not to be one of pride. The right hand 'teaches' (torekha, from yarah, the root behind torah): the king's own arm instructs him in deeds that inspire awe. The KJV's 'terrible things' is a time-bound word for what we would call 'awe-inspiring'. Rashi reads the teaching as the Torah's lesson in tactics, Metzudat David as a hand that learned without any other helper.

philological_notes.note: Either a construct 'humility of righteousness' or two nouns 'humility, righteousness'. Ibn Ezra says it may stand 'between' (separate) or in construct, with the sense 'humility with righteousness'. Radak notes the spelling 'anvah' where a construct would be 'anvat'.

From yarah 'to teach'. Ibn Ezra reports R. Yose's view that it comes from yarah 'to shoot' (as in 'and God shot them', cf. 'your arrows' in the next verse) and sets it aside as fitting a bad sense, while here the sense is praise. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'and will teach you'.
'Things to be feared, awesome acts'; the same word is used of God's wonders at the Exodus.

verses.translation_literal: Your arrows are sharpened; peoples fall under you; [they fall] in the heart of the enemies of the king.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your arrows are whetted to a point. Whole peoples sink beneath your feet, and the arrows lodge deep in the hearts of the king's enemies.
verses.directors_commentary: The grammar here is deliberately tight. The verb yipelu ('they fall') sits in the middle and serves two clauses at once: peoples fall under you, and arrows fall in the enemy's heart. Radak and Ibn Ezra both say so, which is why the accent over it is a half-pause. The KJV pins the phrase to the arrows ('sharp in the heart') and then tacks on 'whereby the people fall', which reverses the sense; the Hebrew has no 'whereby'. 'Heart' (lev) is the center of the body, so the target is the middle of the chest. Ancient armies used composite bows whose arrows were tipped in bronze or iron and sharpened on whetstones. The poet shifts from 'you' to 'the king' in the third person: the court speaks to the king while also speaking about him, which is a normal device in royal poetry. 'Peoples' is plural and general, not a particular named nation.

philological_notes.note: 'They will fall'; one verb shared by two clauses, 'peoples under you' and 'in the heart of the enemies'.
Sharpened; the same root is used for the sword in Deuteronomy 32:41.

verses.translation_literal: Your throne, O God, [is] for ever and ever; a scepter of uprightness [is] the scepter of your kingdom.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your throne, O God, stands for ever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of straightness, and it is held level.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hardest line in the psalm, and the director must decide how to play it. 'Elohim' can address the king ('your throne, O God', the KJV and all four English versions here), or it can mean 'your throne is a throne of God' (Ibn Ezra, Meiri, who compares 'Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD', 1 Chronicles 29:23), or 'God establishes your throne' (Radak's gloss, 'yakhin elohim'). Rashi reads it as 'judge' and cites Exodus 7:1, where God makes Moses 'god to Pharaoh'. In the ancient Near East, a king was sometimes called divine in court poetry (Egypt and Mesopotamia did this); Israel's psalmists keep the title but treat it as a role. The KJV keeps the vocative without comment, which hides all three alternatives. 'Scepter of uprightness' is a scepter of 'levelness' (mishor), the language of a flat road or a fair judgment, the opposite of crookedness. The scepter was a short rod or staff of office; Metzudat Zion notes shevet is also the rod of discipline.

philological_notes.note: Ambiguous: vocative 'O God'; 'your throne of God' (a construct with the first noun carrying the pronoun, Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare 'and the prophecy Oded the prophet'); or 'God will establish your throne' (Radak). Rashi takes 'elohim' as 'judge', after Exodus 7:1.
'Levelness, straightness, equity'; used of a level plain and of fair judgment.

verses.translation_literal: You have loved righteousness and you have hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you, [with] the oil of joy, more than your companions.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have loved what is right, and you have hated what is wrong. For this, God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness, and set you high above your companions.
verses.directors_commentary: Anointing with oil was how an Israelite king was installed (Samuel with Saul, Samuel with David), and oil was also poured at feasts as a sign of gladness; this verse fuses the two, 'oil of joy'. The 'therefore' again links merit to election. The KJV is right here: 'God, thy God' is an exact rendering of the doubled 'Elohim Eloheikha'. Note that the divine name YHWH does not appear: the Hebrew has the common noun twice, which shows the king has a personal relationship with the deity, a point that matters for the 'O God' of verse 7. The final word 'mechaverekha' is 'more than your companions' or 'from among your companions', and the KJV 'above thy fellows' hits the comparison but is unspecific. Ibn Ezra asks whom the companions are: Saul if the king is David, or other devout men in the age of the Messiah. Radak reads 'from among your companions' as the moment of choosing.

philological_notes.note: 'Oil of joy': the festal and royal anointing oil; Isaiah 61:3 uses the same phrase of mourners.
Comparative or partitive min: 'more than' or 'from among' your companions.

verses.translation_literal: Myrrh and aloes, cassia, [are] all your garments; from palaces of ivory, stringed [instruments] have made you glad.
verses.translation_dramatic: Myrrh, aloes and cassia breathe from every fold of your robes. From the ivory halls, strings have made you glad.
verses.directors_commentary: The scene moves to the senses: smell and sound. Myrrh, aloes and cassia were imported spices, expensive and used in oils and incense (Exodus 30:23-24 for myrrh and cassia), so perfumed clothes were a sign of royal wealth, not just good manners. The Hebrew has no verb of smelling: 'myrrh and aloes, cassia, all your garments' is a bare list, and the KJV supplies 'smell of'. 'Palaces of ivory' are halls inlaid with carved ivory panels, like those excavated at Samaria and referred to in 1 Kings 22:39 and Amos 3:15. The final phrase is hard. 'Minni' can be 'stringed instruments' (the usual reading, and the KJV-ASV one), which gives a picture of palace music; but Radak and Metzudat Zion read a 'min' with an extra yod, 'from which', as in 'the halls from which they have made you glad'. Ibn Ezra rejects a place name. The KJV's 'whereby they have made thee glad' follows that second sense; its 'ivory palaces' is a fair translation.

philological_notes.note: Most likely 'stringed instruments' (cf. Psalm 150:4 minnim). Radak and Metzudat Zion read an extra yod, 'min', 'from which'. Ibn Ezra rejects the view that it names a nation or place.
Aloes, a fragrant wood resin; Ibn Ezra cites 'like aloes the LORD planted' (Numbers 24:6) against a marine-source claim.
Cassia; Rashi says the Targum renders 'qiddah' (Exodus 30:24) as 'qetzi'ata'.

verses.translation_literal: Daughters of kings [are] among your precious ones; a queen consort stands at your right, in gold of Ophir.
verses.translation_dramatic: Daughters of kings are among your honored women, and at your right hand stands the queen, in gold from Ophir.
verses.directors_commentary: The court is assembled around the king, and the poet counts rank by position. Royal daughters in the harem or the entourage were the usual marks of a treaty: kings gave their daughters to seal alliances (1 Kings 3:1, Solomon and Pharaoh's daughter). 'Shegal' is a rare word for the principal wife (Nehemiah 2:6; Daniel 5:2-3 in Aramaic); Ibn Ezra and Radak tie it to the root 'to lie with', so the KJV's plain 'queen' blurs a word that also meant 'bed-wife', the one set apart for the king. The right hand was the place of honor. 'Gold of Ophir' was the finest gold in the Bible, shipped by Solomon's fleet (1 Kings 9:28). The KJV's 'honourable women' follows 'yaqar', precious; Rashi (on 45:9) prefers a form from 'to visit' because of the dagesh in the qof. The verse says nothing about her being a convert.

philological_notes.note: A royal consort; Rashi cites Nehemiah 2:6 and Daniel 5:2; Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra link it to a root meaning 'to lie with'.
'Among your precious ones'. The doubled qof led Rashi to read it from 'to visit' (biqqur); Ibn Ezra insists the yod proves 'precious'.
Ketem is fine, probably refined, gold; Ophir was a distant source of gold (1 Kings 9:28).

verses.translation_literal: Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and the house of your father.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen, daughter, and look. Bend your ear to me. Forget your people, forget the house of your father.
verses.directors_commentary: The poet now turns to a 'daughter'. The three imperatives, 'hear, see, incline the ear', are what a teacher or a father says before a farewell: a formal charge. 'Daughter' (bat) is a term of address, and the tradition splits on who she is. Ibn Ezra, on his reading that the psalm is about David, and Malbim make her a bride who must become a convert; Rashi and the Targum read 'daughter' as the Congregation of Israel; Radak and Metzudat David hear it said to each of the royal daughters and each community in turn. The Hebrew only says 'daughter'. The KJV's 'consider' loses the visual verb: ra'i is 'see'. The demand to 'forget your people and your father's house' is stark. In the ancient world a woman moved into her husband's household at marriage, and a foreign princess gave up her own gods and her family's claim on her. Abraham was told to leave his father's house (Genesis 12:1), and Ruth left her people (Ruth 1:16). The KJV adds 'also', which is not in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: 'Forget': a call to leave, not a failure of memory. Ibn Ezra compares 'your people shall be my people' (Ruth 1:16) in his reading of the bride as a convert.

'Daughter' here is an address. Metzudat Zion takes it as 'community', as in 'daughter of Babylon' (Psalm 137:8); Radak takes it as said to each of the kings' daughters of verse 10; Rashi and the Targum read the Congregation of Israel.

verses.translation_literal: And the king will desire your beauty; for he [is] your lord; and bow down to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the king will long for your beauty. He is your lord, so bow yourself down before him.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse gives the reason for the command in verse 11, in a form that sounds like a bargain: if she forgets her family, the king will desire her. The jussive 'yit'av' ('let him desire') is a wish or consequence, so the KJV's 'so shall the king greatly desire' reads it as a promise, which is fair, though 'greatly' is the translator's addition. 'Adonayikh' is a plural of majesty, 'your lord', and it is here the ordinary word for husband or master, not the divine title, though it shares its form. 'Hishtachavi' is the verb for bowing flat to the ground, used before kings and before God; the KJV 'worship thou him' has a religious sense that the Hebrew allows but in a court setting it is homage. Radak insists the point is that she has no other lord, even if she comes from another people; Malbim reads the bride's true beauty as the king's lordship over her.

philological_notes.note: A plural of majesty with a feminine suffix: 'your lord'. Radak says it means she has no other lord.
To bow to the ground; homage to a king as well as worship of God.

verses.translation_literal: And daughter of Tyre, with a gift, your face they will soften, rich ones of a people.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Tyre comes with a gift. The rich of the people will seek to soften your face.
verses.directors_commentary: Tyre was the richest port of the eastern Mediterranean, the city whose purple dye and cedar and ships made kings envious. To say that Tyre brings a gift is to say that money bows to the throne: the poem's picture of the wedding is also a picture of the world's wealth arriving. 'Daughter of Tyre' is the Hebrew way of speaking of a city as a woman, as in 'daughter of Zion'. The grammar is loose: a singular noun with a plural verb, so it is read as the people of Tyre (Radak, Metzudat David), or as an address to the daughter of Tyre (Meiri, Malbim), with 'the rich of a people' as the givers. The KJV adds 'shall be there', which the Hebrew does not say. It also gives 'entreat thy favour'; the Hebrew is more physical: chillah panim, 'to soften the face', as one calms a stern master. The rich do not simply ask; they try to change the expression on the face of someone more powerful than they are. The ASV's 'favor' and the BBE's 'approval' lose that. Mind the gender: 'your face' is feminine, so it is the queen's face that is softened, not the king's.

philological_notes.note: The idiom 'to soften the face' (chillah panim) means to appease or to seek favour by a gift or a request; Rashi ties the verb to Moses' pleading before God (Exod 32:11). Here it is addressed to a woman ('your face', feminine).

'Daughter of Tyre': the city personified as a daughter, as 'daughter of Zion' and 'daughter of Babylon' elsewhere. Radak and Metzudat David take it as the people of Tyre; Meiri and Malbim as a direct address.

verses.translation_literal: All glorious [is the] king's daughter within; of settings of gold [is] her clothing.
verses.translation_dramatic: All glorious is the king's daughter, there within; and her robes are of gold in its settings.
verses.directors_commentary: The camera now moves from the crowd outside to the king's daughter. 'Within' (penimah) is a spatial word and the commentators read it so: Radak has her 'standing within, in the hall', Metzudat David 'sitting within in her chamber', Ibn Ezra living inside her palace and not seen by all. A king's daughter did not walk in public before the wedding; she was kept in the women's quarters. The KJV's 'all glorious within' is right on the first word: kevuddah is 'glorious, honoured', a feminine adjective, not 'her glory'. A possessive would carry a mappiq in the final he (kevodah), which is missing here, and Radak notes the dagesh in the dalet. Where the KJV goes wrong is only in the sermon it invites: 'within' is not 'inner worth' but 'inside the palace'. Her clothing is 'from settings of gold'. The rare word mishbetzot is the word for the gold settings that held the stones of the high priest's ephod (Exod 28), so the picture is of a garment in which gold is woven or set, enormously heavy and costly. Rashi makes that comparison to the high priests' settings. The KJV's 'wrought gold' is acceptable but hides the link to temple furnishings. In this world a king's daughter was worn as wealth: the gold on her body announced her father's treasury.

philological_notes.note: A feminine adjective, 'glorious, honoured', as STEPBible parses it (HAcfsa). It is not 'her glory': that would be kevodah with a mappiq in the final he, and the form here has a dagesh in the dalet and no mappiq. Radak and Metzudat David both read it as 'the honoured one' who is inside the palace.

A rare plural noun, 'settings' (of stones in gold), as in the ephod's gold mountings in Exodus; here applied to cloth worked or set with gold. Metzudat Zion glosses it as the place where precious stones sit; Rashi compares the settings of the high priests.

verses.translation_literal: To embroidered robes she is led to the king; virgins behind her, her companions, are brought to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: In garments of colored thread she is led to the king, slowly, as the song itself is led. Behind her walk the maidens, her own companions, and one by one they are brought to you.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the procession. The bride is 'led' (tuval, the same verb used of gifts and offerings carried to a ruler; Isa 18:7), which sounds passive to modern ears and is ceremonial in the ancient one: a marriage between royal houses was a matter between fathers and kings, and the woman is delivered, with her train, as part of the settlement. 'Embroidered' (riqma) refers to multicolored cloth, with threads of different colors worked in by needle or loom, among the most expensive fabrics there were, and the word is used of the cloth of the Tabernacle and of the dress of captive women in Judges 5:30. The KJV's 'raiment of needlework' gets that. The preposition is a puzzle: 'to embroidered robes' reads literally 'to', and Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri take the lamed as 'in', a common Hebrew substitution, so 'in embroidered robes'. The virgins are bridal attendants, and the word rendered 'companions' is a feminine noun of friendship. The last word is where the voice changes: 'to you' is masculine, so the poet turns back to the king, and the maidens too are 'brought to you'. The KJV hides the sudden address by keeping 'unto the king' and 'unto thee' in the same grammatical frame as if nothing had happened; in the Hebrew the singer simply steps from describing the king to speaking to him.

philological_notes.note: A Hophal of yaval, 'to bring, lead, carry'. The verb is used of bringing gifts to a ruler (Isa 18:7, Ps 68:30), so the bride's arrival is presented as a formal delivery to the king.

'Embroidered [cloth]', multicolored needlework. The lamed is probably 'in' (so Radak, Meiri comparing Gen 4:23, 'I killed a man for [= in] my wound'); I kept 'to' in the literal layer to show the word as written.

verses.translation_literal: They are led with joys and rejoicing; they go into [the] palace of [the] king.
verses.translation_dramatic: They are led in with joy, with a shout of rejoicing, and the doors of the king's great house open and take them in.
verses.directors_commentary: The procession reaches its end: the same verb, 'they are led', carries over from the verse before, so the procession keeps one rhythm through two verses; keep the repetition of tuval audible. 'Joys' is plural in the Hebrew (simchot), an intensifying plural, and it is paired with gil, 'rejoicing', a word that suggests spinning or leaping, with dance in it. The KJV 'gladness and rejoicing' is fine, but it flattens a plural and puts the first verb in the future ('shall they be brought') as if prophesying, whereas the Hebrew is an imperfect that works equally well as a description of what is happening in front of the singer. The 'palace' (heikhal) is a loan from Akkadian ekallu, 'great house', and it is also the word for the temple's main hall: in the royal wedding the language of palace and sanctuary overlap, which is part of why later readers heard something more than a wedding. The last word, 'king', has no article in Hebrew: it is simply 'palace of king', the sort of compressed phrase that suits a song.

philological_notes.note: 'Palace' or 'great hall'; borrowed from Sumerian e-gal through Akkadian ekallu, 'great house'. It is also the word for the main hall of the Jerusalem temple, so the vocabulary of palace and temple overlaps.

verses.translation_literal: In place of your fathers will be your sons; you will set them as princes in all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Where your fathers stood, your sons will stand; and you will set them over the land as princes, in every corner of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The poem now looks past the wedding to the point of the wedding: heirs. A royal marriage was a dynastic contract, and its reward was sons. 'In place of your fathers' means that the king's sons will occupy the seats the ancestors held; it is the language of succession, and this psalm is probably an old court song for a royal wedding. The phrase 'princes in all the earth' is bolder: not one throne, but sons spread as governors across a wide realm, as the sons of an imperial house were. The KJV 'mayest make' turns a plain future ('you will make them') into a possibility and makes the promise a permission; the BBE's 'so that you may make them rulers' does the same and also invents a purpose clause. The Hebrew simply has 'you will set them' (the same verb as setting a person in a position). 'Earth' or 'land' (eretz) is ambiguous: a modern reader hears the planet, but the ancient reader hears 'the land', the whole territory under the king's power; I keep the two in the layers. Note the second-person 'you' is masculine again: the poet speaks to the king.

philological_notes.note: 'You will set them': the verb shit, 'to set, place, appoint', with the archaic poetic suffix -mo for 'them'. The same suffix is found in Exod 15 and elsewhere in poetry, a mark of old poetic style.

verses.translation_literal: I will cause your name to be remembered in every generation and generation; therefore peoples will give thanks to you for ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, the singer, will make your name remembered, in every generation after generation. So the nations will give thanks to you, for ever, and for ever still.
verses.directors_commentary: The poet who began as a quick-writing scribe in verse 2 returns at the end in the first person: the song itself is the means by which the king's name will be remembered. In the ancient Near East, to 'cause a name to be remembered' (hizkir shem) was the work of a court poet or an inscription: the king gave the commission and the poet gave the fame. The verb is causative, 'I will make [it] remembered', and the KJV 'I will make thy name to be remembered' does catch that; the YLT's 'I make mention' loses it. The verse ends with a pun the KJV cannot carry: yehoduka, 'they will give thanks to you', and yehudah, 'Judah', come from the same root, yadah, which is why Jacob's blessing in Gen 49:8 says 'Judah, your brothers will praise you', and why the verse is often heard as a blessing on the royal tribe. KJV 'the people shall praise thee' is a plural 'peoples' reduced to a singular: the Hebrew says 'peoples', in the plural, and it is a claim of universal reach, as in the Tyrian gift at the start of the scene. The closing 'for ever and ever' is 'le'olam va'ed', a stock expression for continuous time with no end in sight.

philological_notes.note: A Hiphil cohortative, 'let me cause to be remembered', 'I will make remembered'. To make a name remembered is the work of the court poet or the monument.

'They will give thanks to you', Hiphil of yadah, 'to throw, thank, praise'. The root is the one behind the name Judah (Gen 29:35), and Gen 49:8 plays on it: 'Judah, your brothers will praise you.' Meiri cites that verse in his comment on this one.
